name: Fuhrer Thumb
approach: South-southwest from trailhead via Nisqually Moraine descent to Nisqually Glacier, cross glacier westward, ascend Wilson Gully/Wilson Bench/Wilson Chute on west side of glacier to Lower Castle camp, then continue northwest to Fuhrer Thumb couloir

approach_variants.name: Paradise, the Nisqually crossing and the Wilson Glacier to the narrow couloir
approach_variants.notes:
From Paradise, drop southwest onto the Nisqually Moraine and onto the Nisqually Glacier, cross it westward, then work up the Wilson Gully, the Wilson Bench and the Wilson Chute on the west side of the glacier toward the camps near The Castle around 9,000-9,500 ft.

From camp, continue northwest to the foot of the couloir. Summit day from that camp is commonly 5 to 7 hours.

The couloir is about 50-degree snow and ice. It merges with the Fuhrer Finger on the west side of the Nisqually at roughly 11,500 ft, so above that point the two routes are one.

Most parties descend the Fuhrer Finger or the upper Kautz and the standard route back to Camp Muir and Paradise rather than reversing this line. There is no water above Paradise.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr-Jun; a south-facing snow line that wants a hard overnight freeze and an early start
hazards: Rockfall funnelling through a steep, narrow couloir with no shelter in it
Icefall off the Kautz Ice Cliff onto the approach traverse
Wet-snow avalanche on this south aspect once it warms — an early start is the protection
Crevasses on the Nisqually and Wilson glaciers
The Finger and the Thumb merge high, so a misidentification cannot be detected above 11,500 ft
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Stand on the upper Wilson Glacier and look up. From left to right the three features are: the Wilson Glacier headwall, the Fuhrer Thumb, the Fuhrer Finger. Learn that order before you leave the car — it is the only thing separating this route from its two neighbours in the dark, and all three start within a short distance of each other off the same bench of glacier.

The Thumb is the middle one and it is the narrow one. That is the whole test, and it is a shape test, which is what you want when you cannot see the mountain.

The positive-negative pair that settles it: the Finger is wide and funnels through an obvious hourglass at around 10,000 ft on the eastern side of the headwall. The Thumb is the narrower couloir immediately west of it. So if the gully in front of you is broad and necks down through a conspicuous hourglass, you are at the Finger and the Thumb is one gully to your left as you face uphill. If you are looking at an open face rather than into a gully at all, you have gone one too far left and you are under the Wilson Glacier Headwall, which is a harder proposition than either couloir.

Confirmation on the climb: the two couloirs merge at about 11,500 ft on the west side of the Nisqually. So being one gully out becomes invisible above that height, which cuts both ways — it means a mistake is survivable, and it means you cannot use the upper mountain to work out which one you climbed. Settle it at the bottom.

What being too early in the approach looks like: if you have not crossed the Nisqually Glacier westward, you have not started. Everything about this route is on the west side of that glacier, under The Castle and the Kautz Ice Cliff.
